meta.title: Water That Follows the Moon
meta.skill_frame: Find the main idea: decide what a whole passage is mostly about, not one true detail.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fifth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.8 on the three parts together, inside the grade 4-5 band. The load is one chain of cause: gravity makes a bulge, the planet turns, a coast passes through it.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from NOAA NESDIS, 'What Causes Tides?'
source.attribution: U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, NESDIS, 'What Causes Tides?', https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/about/k-12-education/oceans-coasts/what-causes-tides, accessed 2026-11-15. U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
source.text_status: Adapted, reading load reduced by splitting long sentences.
source.survey: The moon's gravity moves ocean water into two bulges, and Earth's rotation carries coastlines through them twice a day.
source.avoided: No explanation of the far-side bulge beyond what the page states; no tidal range figures.

session.difficulty_basis: How far the stated idea sits from the words the passage uses.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: High tides and low tides are caused by the moon. The moon’s gravitational pull generates something called the tidal force. This tidal force causes Earth, and its water, to bulge out on the side closest to the moon and on the side farthest from the moon. These bulges of water are high tides. As Earth rotates, your region of Earth passes through both of these bulges each day. When you are in one of the bulges, you experience a high tide. When you are not in one of the bulges, you experience a low tide. This cycle of two high tides and two low tides occurs most days on most of the coastlines of the world.
passage.part_2: Tides are really all about gravity. When we talk about the daily tides, it is the moon’s gravity that causes them. As Earth rotates, the moon’s gravity pulls on different parts of our planet. The moon only has about one hundredth the mass of Earth. Since it is so close to us, it has enough gravity to move things around. The moon’s gravity even pulls on the land, but not enough for anyone to tell. When the moon’s gravity pulls on the water in the oceans, someone is bound to notice. Water has a much easier time moving around, and it wants to bulge in the direction of the moon.
passage.part_3: Because of the tidal force, the water on the side of the moon always wants to bulge out toward the moon. The tidal force causes Earth and its water to bulge on the side closest to the moon and on the side farthest from the moon. These bulges of water are high tides. As Earth rotates, your region passes through both bulges each day. When you are in one of the bulges, you experience a high tide. When you are not in one of the bulges, you experience a low tide. This cycle of two high tides and two low tides occurs most days on most coastlines of the world.
